extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of art history, literary criticism, and educated general readers interested in Renaissance painting
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical-critical criteria for assessing the style, temperament, and artistic methods of Renaissance painters (especially Michelangelo and Leonardo) as presented in a literary-essay format. Focuses on aesthetic qualities, artistic temperament, methods of study, and expressive aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preoccupation with death
rubrics_metrics.description: All the great Florentines were preoccupied with death; an outward seriousness and 'Outre-tombe' sentiment is a dignifying, high-quality trait.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as a cultural and emotional disposition informing subject-matter and tone (tombs, funerary sculpture, responsive pathos). Examples: tombs in San Miniato, Botticelli painting executed conspirators, meditation over lifeless bodies leading to simplified, dignified lines. This preoccupation should manifest as gravity rather than morbid grotesqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity (Pietà) as central emotional aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Pity—exemplified in the Pietà and entombment—is Michelangelo's predilection: 'mere pity and awe at the stiff limbs and colourless lips' rather than divine sorrow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works should convey human, hopeless, rayless sorrow and tender pity; sculpture and composition emphasize the physical reality of loss rather than theological consolation. Examples: various sketches and unfinished groups centered on the entombment and the Virgin's pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of sweetness and strength
rubrics_metrics.description: A defining quality of Michelangelo is the strange interfusion of sweetness and strength in his work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The balance of gentleness and force must be moderated — neither sacrificially sweet nor merely muscular. This mixture distinguishes great masters and helps place other talents by comparison (e.g., Blake, Victor Hugo cited as spiritual descendants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional pictorial conceptions as inherited 'types'
rubrics_metrics.description: Medieval/earlier pictorial conceptions (legends, iconic types) can exist independently and be handed on with minor change; the artist inherits and finalises them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should note how an artist receives and transforms inherited types (e.g., central conception from tradition to Sistine Chapel frescoes). Distinguish between original invention and masterful reworking of tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vague, musical suggestion over definite symbolism
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures such as Michelangelo's Night and Day express vague fancies, presentiments, and musical promptings rather than fixed symbolic meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer readings that emphasize shifting, mixed, and indefinable sentiments communicated by touch and tone rather than rigid allegorical labels; sacristy works aim for wistful speculation, solemnity, not consolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mature, dispassionate inquiry into immortality
rubrics_metrics.description: Michelangelo's outlook is cautious and based on 'consciousness of ignorance' about the spiritual world; hope is tentative and speculative rather than formal or childlike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should reflect a grown, philosophical uncertainty — restrained, hesitant glimmers of hope rather than doctrinal certainty (contrast with Dante).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fascination, mystery, and enigma
rubrics_metrics.description: Leonardo's work is characterised by a 'mystery in his work' and something enigmatical beyond the usual measure of great men; he fascinates by refined and graceful mystery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should look for an exotic, enigmatic quality that invites fascination more than straightforward delight. This trait may make the artist seem to possess 'unsanctified and sacred wisdom.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sudden revolts, intermittent productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Leonardo's life shows 'sudden revolts, with intervals in which he works not at all'—a temperament that clusters chief work into a few intense, tormented years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an oeuvre, account for irregular production rhythms: long pauses, reworking, and concentrated bursts of major works are part of his character and influence the condition and completeness of works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curiosity and desire of beauty as dual forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Two elementary forces in Leonardo's genius are curiosity (boundless inquiry) and the desire of beauty; their union generates a subtle and curious grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good work reconciles or productively tensions scientific curiosity and aesthetic sensibility. Note where curiosity deepens pictorial invention and where it conflicts with beauty (overdetail, anatomical fixation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Return to nature (observation) over return to antiquity
rubrics_metrics.description: Leonardo represents a 'return to nature'—seeking microscopic finish and subtler law in natural phenomena—whereas others (e.g., Raffaelle) return to antiquity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuate paintings by their fidelity to, and insightful selection from, nature: attention to natural correspondences, refinement of atmospheric and landscape effects, and the naturalistic modelling of forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopic sense of finish ('subtilitas naturae')
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'microscopic sense of finish'—delicate, refined detail and finesse—characterises Leonardo's approach to nature and pictorial effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess fine-grained handling (e.g., leaves, flowers, water surfaces) and subtle atmospheric gradations. Examples: studies of violets, cyclamen; delicate rendering of water and shells in La Gioconda and Saint Anne.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intimate presence in objects and figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Leonardo learned 'the art of going deep, of tracking the sources of expression to their subtlest retreats' and acquired 'the power of an intimate presence in the things he handled.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should convey an inward, concentrated knowledge of the subject — not only surface likeness but the thing's inner life (seen in portraits and close studies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste for the bizarre and recherché in landscape
rubrics_metrics.description: A taste for what is bizarre or recherché in landscape—strange, hollow places, ridged trap-rocks, and odd atmospheric effects—is characteristic of Leonardo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Landscape should be selective and uncanny: places 'far withdrawn' and hours chosen for finesse, not generic or merely decorative backgrounds. Evaluate the specificity and distinctness of landscape invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraiture: embodiment of reality 'on dark air'
rubrics_metrics.description: Leonardo is 'above all a painter of portraits; faces of a modelling more skilful... embodied with a reality which almost amounts to illusion, on dark air.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess portraits for their nuanced modelling, atmospheric integration, and the painter's ability to 'sound the stops' of character. Examples: Ludovico, Lucretia Crivelli, Beatrice d'Este portraits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict between scientific curiosity and pictorial beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Leonardo's curiosity sometimes 'went too far below that outside of things in which art begins and ends', creating tension that can mar beauty (overdetail, re-touching, unfinished works).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good evaluation notes when inquiry enriches art vs. when it overwhelms aesthetic form; watch for signs of overstudy, endless reworking, or an 'air of weariness and ennui' in the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiting for the 'moment of bien-etre' (moment of invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leonardo will not work 'till the happy moment comes' — the siezure of invention (bien-etre) when idea is struck into colour and image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess creative acts for evidence of inspired unification rather than mere technical competence; finished works should show that the decisive moment of synthesis was reached. Many flaws stem from working outside that moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmutation of ideas into images
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist's task is the transmutation of ideas into images; success is when the cloudy mysticism is refined into a subdued and graceful mystery that pleases eye and satisfies soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the degree to which concept/idea has been materially and poetically transformed into a coherent visual effect. Look for refined mystery and unified pictorial effect (e.g., sfumato, tonal harmony).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract grace of bounding lines (drawing quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leonardo's drawings exhibit a curious beauty in the 'abstract grace of the bounding lines' — contours and poises that belong peculiarly to art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess line as expressive contour: hair, head curves, posture, and the poise of limbs. Examples include red chalk heads and studies showing maternal feeling and pathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathos, maternity, and human sentiment in figure-drawing
rubrics_metrics.description: A feeling for maternity and the capacity to convey pathos (e.g., child and mother heads, small Madonnas) is characteristic and essential to affective power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate tenderness, proportioned emotional detail, and small gestures (rounded shoulders, stooping posture) that produce convincing pathos without sentimentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ostensible subject as pretext for subtle sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Leonardo often uses sacred or conventional subjects merely as starting-points for trains of sentiment 'as subtle and vague as a piece of music' rather than literal depiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether subject-matter is subordinated to an overarching mood or musical sequence of feeling (e.g., Saint John the Baptist resembling Bacchus), and whether that transformation is artistically coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesque and fascination with corruption as expressive device
rubrics_metrics.description: Leonardo can fuse beauty and terror (e.g., the Medusa), where the fascination of corruption penetrates every touch within exquisitely finished beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how grotesque elements are balanced with finish and poise; whether the grotesque informs a deeper insight rather than becoming mere sensationalism. Example: Medusa as corpse-head whose features and surrounding snakes are rendered with exquisite finish.
